> Thanks for the conversation earlier. To capture it: we agreed deliverable dates hold, with a heads-up by the prior Wednesday if anything's at risk. Let's check in on the 20th. Let me know if I've missed anything.

## Avoid
- "Some people have said..."
- "You always / you never."
- Feedback by email when it should be a conversation.
- Piling several issues into one meeting.
- Ending without a clear ask.
- Not following up. Silence after feedback reads as "it didn't matter."

## If they push back or the behaviour doesn't change
Pushback with new context is useful: listen, then restate the ask if it still stands. Pushback that is only heat ("that's unfair", "everyone does that") gets a calm, short repeat and a close, not a debate. If nothing has changed by the check-in date, say so plainly, make the consequence clear, and put it in writing. Escalate through the right channel (your manager, HR) rather than having the same conversation a fourth time.
> I hear that you see it differently. The ask stands: dates hold, or a heads-up by the Wednesday before. Let's see how the next two weeks go and talk on the 20th.
> We agreed on the 6th that deadlines would hold, and the last two have slipped again. I need this to change now, and I'll be tracking it in our one-to-ones. What's getting in the way?

entries.title: Group chats: organising plans, chasing decisions, handling flakes
triggers: nobody replies in the group chat
entries.summary: How to get a group to actually decide: fewer options, deadlines, a named default, and gentle ways to handle the person who always bails.
entries.body:
# Group chats: organising and deciding

## Goal
The group reaches a decision that sticks, in the fewest messages, and nobody feels nagged or steamrolled.

## Structure
1. **Propose one concrete plan** (date, time, place), or two options at most.
2. **Ask for a one-tap reply** (thumbs up, yes/no).
3. **Set a deadline and say what happens by default** if people go quiet.
4. **Confirm the decision in one message** once you have it, then move logistics to a smaller thread.

## Why groups stall
Nobody replies because replying feels like committing, and everyone assumes someone else will. Fix: make the reply tiny, give a deadline, and name what happens if nobody answers.

## Principles
- **Propose, don't ask.** "Saturday 7pm at Luca's, who's in?" beats "what does everyone want to do?"
- **Two options, max.** A poll with two choices gets answered; one with six gets ignored.
- **Deadline with a default.** "I'll book for 6 on Thursday unless I hear otherwise."
- **Ask for a specific reaction.** "Thumbs up if in" makes it a one-tap reply.
- **Name people when you need them.** "@Sam @Priya you two haven't said" is fine if warm.
- **Move logistics to a smaller thread** once the plan is set.

## Examples

**Kick off a plan:**
> Right, birthday dinner for Jo. Proposal: Saturday 14th, 7:30, Bar Italia. 👍 if you're in, 👎 if you can't, by Wednesday please so I can book. Silence means I assume yes and you're paying for a chair.

**Chase a stalled decision:**
> Gentle nudge: still need to lock the date. Two options: the 14th or the 21st. Thumbs on the one you prefer. Deciding tomorrow night.

**Trip planning, first message:**
> Trip: I'm proposing Lisbon, 10 to 14 October, budget around $600 each all in. This is a real proposal, not a wish; if three people say yes by Friday I'll book the flat. Say yes, no, or "different dates".

**Someone keeps flaking, address in the group (light):**
> @Tom you're on your third "maybe next time", we're starting a tally. Genuinely, come Saturday, it's not the same without you.

**Someone keeps flaking, address privately (real):**
> Hey, not a big deal but you've bailed on the last few things and I'm starting to plan around you not coming. If things are hard right now, tell me and I'll stop pestering. If you just don't fancy the group stuff, that's fine too, I'd just rather know.

**Cutting through a long argument about where to eat:**
> Okay, executive decision: Thai place, 7:30. Anyone who objects can pick next time.

**Group chat that's become too noisy:**
> Suggestion: let's keep this one for plans and start a separate chat for the memes. I keep missing actual info.

**Leaving a plan you'd agreed to:**
> I've got to drop out of Saturday, sorry all. Don't change anything for me. Next one, I promise.

**Asking people to pay their share:**
> Booking's done, $85 each. My link is [link]; no rush but before the 10th please so I'm not out of pocket for weeks.

## Avoid
- "What does everyone think?"
- Open-ended questions with no deadline.
- Re-asking the same question when nobody replied; change the question.
- Passive-aggressive "guess nobody's interested then".
- Making the decision, then reopening it because one person complained.
- Chasing in the group when it's really about one person.

## If nobody replies, or someone reopens it
Silence past the deadline: do what you said you would and post it once. Do not re-ask. If someone complains after the decision, acknowledge it, hold the plan, and hand them the next one. If the thread turns into an argument between two people, message each of them directly rather than refereeing in the group. If a flake drops out late again, quietly stop planning around them; announcing it in the group only makes everyone else uncomfortable.
> Deadline was tonight, so I've booked Bar Italia for 6 at 7:30. If you didn't say and want in, message me by tomorrow and I'll ask for an extra seat.
> Fair, Thai isn't everyone's first pick. It's booked now, so you choose next time.

entries.title: Handling a client or prospect who went silent
triggers: they ghosted me after the proposal
entries.summary: How to re-engage a silent client or prospect without desperation, and how to close the loop cleanly when it's over.
entries.body:
# Client or prospect went silent

## Goal
Either they re-engage because you made it easy, or you close the file cleanly and stop spending energy on it. Both are wins.

## Principles
- Silence after a proposal usually means: priorities shifted, budget got cut, they're embarrassed to say no, or your email is buried. Almost never personal.
- Each follow-up should make replying easier than the last: fewer options, smaller ask.
- Offer the no explicitly. People ghost because they hate saying no; give them a one-word way to do it.
- Three touches, then a clean close. The close often gets a reply.
- Add value in at least one follow-up. New information gives them a reason to reply that is not "sorry I ignored you".

## The sequence

**Touch 1 (one week after silence): assume buried.**
> Hi Ravi, bumping the proposal from the 3rd in case it got lost. Happy to adjust anything. Would it help to have a 15-minute call to go through it, or would you rather I just answer questions by email?

**Touch 2 (two weeks later): add value, shrink the ask.**
> Hi Ravi, since I sent the proposal we've finished a similar project for [company] and I thought the results might be useful context: [one line]. Is this still something you're looking at this quarter? A quick yes / no / not yet is all I need.

**Touch 3 (two weeks later): the clean close.**
> Hi Ravi, I'll assume the timing isn't right and close this on my side so I'm not cluttering your inbox. If it comes back up, I'd genuinely like to help; just reply to this thread. Best of luck with [their project].

## Variations

**Existing client who's gone quiet mid-project:**
> Hi Ravi, I haven't heard back on the draft from the 10th and I want to make sure we're still on track. If there's a hold-up on your side, no problem, just let me know so I can plan my schedule. If you'd like me to pause, say the word.

**When you need a decision by a date:**
> I'm holding time for this project in October, and I need to release it to someone else if we're not proceeding. Could you let me know by Friday either way?

**Reply to a "sorry for the silence":**
> No apology needed, I know how it goes. Where would you like to pick up from?

## Avoid
- "Just checking in!" with nothing else.
- "I've tried reaching you several times..."
- Guilt-tripping.
- Following up daily.
- A long re-pitch.
- Leaving it open forever. Close it, it's healthier and often gets a reply.

## If they reply with a no, or come back after the close
A no is the second-best outcome: thank them, ask one question about why if the relationship is warm enough, and leave the door open. Do not counter with a discount you never offered before; it teaches them that silence gets a better price. If they resurface months after the close, skip the reproach entirely and re-scope from today's facts (your availability, current rates), not last year's proposal.
> Thanks for letting me know, I appreciate the clear answer. If it's useful, one line on what tipped it would help me. Either way, good luck with the project.
> Good to hear from you. Happy to pick this up. My availability and rates have moved since March, so let me send a fresh version this week.

entries.title: Handling a no-show or lateness
triggers: I was late and missed it
entries.summary: Messaging someone who flaked, is running late, or keeps cancelling; owning it when you are the one who was late; naming a pattern without an ultimatum; and handling a client or vendor no-show.
entries.body:
# Handling a no-show or lateness

## Goal
The plan gets rescued or rescheduled, the other person knows what you noticed, and nobody has to pretend it did not happen. Warm on the person, clear on the pattern.

## They are running late or did not show (one-off)
1. **Check they are okay.** One line, no sarcasm.
2. **State what you will do.** "I'll wait till 7:30" or "I'm heading off, let's rebook."
3. **Give them a concrete next step** if you still want to meet.

## You were late or did not show
1. **Name it specifically.** "I missed our 6pm" not "sorry about earlier".
2. **Own it without a "but".** Context, if needed, is one clause after the apology.
3. **Acknowledge their cost.** Their time, their evening, the table they held.
4. **Propose a fix with a date.** Do not ask them to do the rescheduling work.
5. **One make-good if it fits.** "Coffee's on me."

## Friend who cancels last minute, repeatedly
1. **Say you enjoy seeing them.** Real, not a softener.
2. **Name the pattern with numbers.** "Three of the last four."
3. **Say the effect on you, one line.** "I stop planning around it."
4. **Ask what would actually work.** Shorter, closer, more spontaneous. Let them tell you.
5. **No ultimatum.** You are adjusting how you plan, not threatening the friendship.

## Professional no-show (client, vendor, contractor)
1. **Factual and dated.** "We had 10am today; I waited until 10:30."
2. **Consequence, if there is one.** Fee, missed slot, delayed timeline. Stated, not threatened.
3. **One rebooking option** with a specific time.
4. **What happens if it recurs**, said once, calmly.

## Principles
- Sarcasm feels good for a minute and costs you the conversation.
- Numbers beat adjectives. "Always" gets argued; "three of the last four" does not.
- Say what you will do, not what they must do. That is the difference between a boundary and a demand.
- If you are the one who flaked, the apology is short and the fix is specific. Long apologies make them comfort you.
- A professional no-show is a business matter. Keep it in business language and put it in writing.

## Examples

**They're 20 minutes late, no word:**
> Hey, all okay? I'm at the table by the window. I'll hang on till 7:30, after that let's do another night.

**They no-showed, one-off:**
> Missed you tonight, hope nothing's wrong. I'm free Thursday or Sunday if you want to try again, your pick.

**You're running late:**
> Running 15 minutes behind, my fault, left too late. Order without me and I'll catch up. There by 7:15.

**You no-showed a friend:**
> I completely missed our lunch today and I'm sorry. No excuse, I had the wrong day in my head. You held a table and gave up your break for it. Can I take you Friday, same place, my treat?

**Friend who cancels last minute, naming the pattern:**
> I love hanging out with you, and the last three plans have all been cancelled the day of. I'm not upset, I just want to find something that works. Would shorter and closer suit better, like a coffee near yours on a weekday? Or tell me what would.

**Friend who is always late, before the next meet-up:**
> Booking 7 for Friday. Fair warning, I'll order at 7:15 whether you're there or not, so I'm not sitting with an empty plate. See you then.

**Client no-show, email:**
> Hi [name], we had a call scheduled for 10am today and I waited until 10:30. No problem if something came up. I can offer Thursday at 2pm or Friday at 11am. Please note that a second missed session without 24 hours' notice is charged at the full rate, as per our agreement.

**Vendor or contractor no-show:**
> Hi [name], you were booked for 9am today and nobody arrived or called. I've taken the morning off for this. Can you confirm a new date by end of tomorrow? If I don't hear back I'll need to book someone else.

## Avoid
- "No worries!" when there are worries. It teaches them the flaking is free.
- "Typical" or "as usual". You lose the moral high ground and the point.
- Asking "why?" They will give a reason and you will have to accept it.
- An ultimatum with a friend. "If you cancel again we're done" makes the next cancellation a crisis.
- Over-apologising when you were late by five minutes. Match the size.
- Waiting silently for an hour then exploding. Set the limit early and out loud.

## If it goes badly
If they get defensive about the pattern:
> I'm not keeping score to punish you. I'd rather say it than quietly stop inviting you. Let's try the coffee idea and see.

If a friend keeps cancelling after you named it, stop making fixed plans and say so, once, without heat:
> No stress at all. I'm going to stop booking things in advance for now, but if you're ever free last minute, text me and I'll come if I can.

If a client argues the no-show fee:
> I understand it's frustrating. The policy was in the agreement you signed, and I apply it to everyone. Thursday at 2 is still open if you'd like it.

entries.title: Handling a refund, return or cancellation request
entries.summary: Saying yes fast when you can, saying no kindly when you must, and offering an alternative either way, without hiding behind policy.
entries.body:
# Handling a refund request

## Goal
Whether the answer is yes or no, the customer feels dealt with fairly and quickly, and would buy from you again. Policy is your reason, never your opening line.

## The decision first
Ask yourself: is the cost of this refund higher than the cost of this customer telling ten people you were difficult? Usually it is not. Say yes when you reasonably can.

## Structure
1. **Acknowledge the specific issue**, in their words.
2. **The answer**: yes, no, or a middle option, in the first two lines.
3. **If yes: exactly what happens and when.**
4. **If no: one-line reason, then the alternative you can offer.**
5. **Sign off warmly, no "policy" language.**

## Examples

**Yes, item arrived damaged:**
> Oh no, I'm sorry the mug arrived cracked, that's not okay. I'll send a replacement today, no need to return the broken one. You'll have tracking by this evening. If you'd rather have a refund instead, just say.

**Yes, changed their mind, within window:**
> No problem at all! Send it back to [address] and I'll refund the full amount the day it arrives. Return label's attached. Sorry it wasn't right for you.

**No, outside return window, offer alternative:**
> Thanks for getting in touch. I can see the order was from March, and our returns close at 30 days, so I can't do a full refund on this one. What I can do is offer store credit for 50% of the price, or a 20% code for your next order. Would either help?

**No, custom / personalised item:**
> I'm sorry it's not what you hoped for. Because this one was made to your spec I'm not able to refund it, since I can't resell it. If there's something specific that's wrong with it, I'd genuinely like to fix it, so tell me what's off.

**Cancellation before shipping:**
> Cancelled and refunded, you'll see it back on your card in 3 to 5 days. Sorry to see you go; if it was something we did, I'd love to know.

**Service cancellation with notice policy:**
> I can cancel Thursday's session for you. Because it's under 24 hours, the deposit isn't refundable, but I'm happy to move it to another day this month instead so you don't lose it. Want to do that?

**Chargeback threat:**
> I'd really rather sort this directly with you than through the bank, and I think we can. Here's what I can offer right now: [option]. If that doesn't work, tell me what would.

## Principles
- Speed defuses. Reply within hours.
- Never open with "Unfortunately" or "As per our policy".
- A partial yes (credit, exchange, discount) turns most nos into acceptable outcomes.
- Do not ask them to prove things unless the amount justifies it.
- Do not argue about whose fault it is.
- Refund fast when you say you will. The delay is the real complaint.

## Avoid
- Copy-pasting the policy.
- Making them fill in a form for a $20 item.
- "We apologise for any inconvenience."
- Silence while you "look into it" for days.
- Defending the product.

## If they escalate, threaten a review or dispute the charge
Reply within hours, in the same calm tone, and restate the best offer you can make in one line. Do not match their heat and do not mention the review unless they do. If they file a chargeback, send the bank your records (order, tracking, messages) and stop negotiating in the thread. If they turn abusive, one line that ends it is enough, and you do not have to keep replying.
> I understand you're frustrated and I'd still like to sort this. The offer is full store credit or a 50% refund, whichever suits you, and I can process either today. Let me know which.
> I've set out the options I can offer. I'm going to leave it there, and the credit stays available if you want it.

entries.title: Introducing yourself (new job, new group, event, online community)
entries.summary: Self-introductions that make people want to talk to you: short, one concrete thing about your work, one human thing, and an invitation.
entries.body:
# Introducing yourself

## Goal
People remember one thing about you and feel invited to reach out. Not a CV. Not a performance.

## Structure
1. **Name and role/reason you're here**, one line.
2. **One concrete thing** about what you do or care about (not "passionate about innovation").
3. **One human thing** that gives people a hook (a hobby, where you're from, an odd fact).
4. **An invitation**: what you'd like to hear from them, or how to reach you.

## Principles
- Under 100 words for written intros. Thirty seconds spoken.
- Specific beats impressive. "I spent last year fixing our checkout flow" beats "I'm a results-driven product leader".
- The human thing is the part people remember. Pick one that invites conversation.
- Say what you want. "I'd love to hear what's annoying you about the current system" makes people talk to you.
- Match the room. A Slack intro is casual; a board intro is not.

## Examples

**New job, Slack or Teams:**
> Hi all, I'm Maya, joining the platform team as an engineer today. Most recently I was at [company] working on payments infrastructure, so if anything payment-shaped is broken, I'm your person. Outside work I'm slowly restoring a 1970s bike and mostly failing. I'd love 15 minutes with anyone who wants to tell me what's annoying about the current system; DMs open.

**First day, spoken to the team:**
> Hi, I'm Maya. I've come from [company] where I spent three years on payments. I'm here to help with the platform rebuild. I'll spend the first couple of weeks mostly listening, so grab me if there's something you think I should know. I'm also new to the city, so restaurant recommendations welcome.

**Online community / forum / Discord:**
> Hey, I'm Sam, a self-taught designer working mostly on tiny apps for local businesses. I joined because I keep getting stuck on onboarding flows and this seems like the place people actually talk about it. I'll mostly lurk to start; if you have a favourite thread on onboarding, point me at it.

**Networking event, spoken:**
> I'm Sam, I do design for small shops, mostly the boring-but-important bits like checkout. What are you working on?

**New to a parents' group, sports club, neighbourhood chat:**
> Hi everyone, I'm Jo, we moved into number 14 last month with two kids (6 and 9) and a very loud dog, sorry in advance. Happy to help with anything neighbourly, and we'd love to know where the good playground is.

**Short bio for a profile or panel:**
> Maya Chen is an engineer on [company]'s platform team, where she spent three years making payments fail less often. Before that she was at [previous]. She lives in Bristol and is slowly restoring a bike that will never be ridden.

**Meeting a client team for the first time:**
> I'm Nina, I'll be leading the design work on this. I've done similar rebuilds for [two names] and the thing I care most about is that it's still easy to use in a year. I'll be asking a lot of questions this week; none of them are traps.

## Avoid
- "Passionate about", "results-driven", "ninja".
- Listing every previous employer.
- Self-deprecation past one line.
- No invitation at the end (dead end).
- Long paragraphs.
- Jokes that need context.

## If the intro gets no response
A quiet channel is normal, especially in a big Slack workspace or a busy Discord. Do not re-post or ask whether anyone saw it. Within a day or two, reply to someone else's message or ask one specific question in a relevant channel; the intro did its job as background. If someone answers with a joke at your expense or a pointed question, take it lightly and answer the real question if there is one.
> Quick one for the platform folks: which of the current on-call runbooks is the least trustworthy? Asking so I know where to start reading.
> Ha, fair. The bike has been "nearly done" for two years. Anyway, what's the current pain point on checkout?

entries.title: Landlords, tenants, contractors and service providers
entries.summary: Firm, documented, polite messages for housing and home-service situations: pushing back on a rent increase, requesting repairs, recovering a deposit, disputing a contractor's work or price.
entries.body:
# Landlords, tenants, contractors and service providers

## Goal
Get the outcome while keeping the relationship workable, because you will need this person again. Everything in writing, everything dated, everything calm.

## Principles
- Written, always. Text or email, never only a call. If you call, follow up with "confirming what we discussed".
- Facts, dates, amounts. Feelings weaken these messages.
- Ask for a specific thing by a specific date.
- Reference the agreement or the law once, neutrally, not as a threat. "Under the lease" is enough.
- Stay pleasant. The person who stays pleasant and precise wins most disputes.
- Escalate in steps: request → reminder with date → formal notice. Never jump to the last step first.

## Rent increase, pushing back

**Do not send a flat no.** A flat refusal to a rent increase usually ends in non-renewal. The move is a counter: a specific number, one or two strong reasons, and an easy way for the landlord to say yes. If the user has not given their current rent, the proposed rent, or comparable prices, ask for them or leave clearly labelled brackets.

**Structure (all four, in order):** thanks for notice → counter with a specific number → one or two reasons that are about facts, not your budget (comparable listings, years in the unit, payment record, condition of the flat) → a concrete ask (sign for 12 months at that number, or a call this week).

**Before sending:** check whether the lease allows an increase before renewal, and ask for any change in writing.

> Hi Mark,
> Thanks for letting me know about the proposed increase to $2,100. I'd like to ask you to reconsider. Comparable units in the building are listing at $1,850 to $1,950, and I've been here three years with rent always on time. I'd be glad to sign another 12 months at $1,900. Would that work for you? Happy to talk it through by phone if easier.
> Best,
> Jess

**If they hold firm:**
> Understood. Could you meet me halfway at $2,000, with the bathroom fan repaired before the new term starts? I'd sign today on that basis.

## Repair request (and follow-up)

**First:**
> Hi Mark, the kitchen tap has been leaking since Monday and it's getting worse; there's water pooling under the sink. Could you arrange a plumber this week? I'm home after 5pm any day, or can leave a key. Photos attached.

**Reminder, one week later:**
> Following up on the tap leak from the 12th. It's now damaging the cabinet base. Could you confirm a repair date by Friday? If it's easier, I can book a plumber and deduct it from rent with your written okay.

**Formal, after two weeks:**
> This is a formal repair request for the kitchen tap leak first reported on 12 May. Under the lease, repairs affecting water and fixtures are the landlord's responsibility. Please confirm a repair date within seven days. I'd much prefer to sort this informally, so do call me.

## Getting a deposit back

> Hi Mark, I moved out on the 30th and left the flat clean with the keys as agreed; photos from the day attached. Could you confirm when the $1,800 deposit will be returned? Under the lease it's due within 14 days. Thanks for the last three years, it was a good place to live.

**If they deduct unfairly:**
> Thanks for the breakdown. I don't agree with the $400 for repainting: the walls were in the same condition as at move-in, per the photos in the inventory and mine attached. Please return that portion. I'm happy to accept the $80 cleaning charge. If we can't agree, I'll raise it with the deposit scheme, but I'd rather settle it directly.

## Contractor: quote too high / work not finished / overcharged

**Quote too high:**
> Thanks for the quote. It's above what I'd budgeted. Is there a way to bring it under $3,000, maybe by dropping [item] or using [alternative]? I'd like to work with you on this.

**Work not finished:**
> Hi Dave, the job was due to finish on the 20th and the tiling in the bathroom is still incomplete. Could you give me a date this week for completion? I'll release the final payment once it's done as agreed.

**Overcharged:**
> The invoice came in at $1,450 against the agreed $1,100. Could you walk me through the difference? If there was extra work I wasn't told about, I'd like to understand it before paying. Happy to pay the agreed $1,100 today.

## Landlord to tenant (the other side)

**Rent increase notice, kind version:**
> Hi Jess, I'm writing to give notice that rent will increase to $2,000 from 1 September, in line with the market and the higher building costs this year. You've been a great tenant and I'd like you to stay. If you'd like to talk it through, I'm around.

**Late rent, first message:**
> Hi Jess, rent for May hasn't come through yet. Could you check on it? If something's changed on your side, let me know and we can work something out.

## Avoid
- "This is unacceptable."
- Threatening legal action in the first message.
- Long emotional histories.
- Withholding rent without written agreement or legal advice.
- Only calling. If it isn't written, it didn't happen.

## If they refuse, ignore you or get hostile
Move one step up the ladder you set out (request, dated reminder, formal notice), never two. Reply in writing even if they call, and keep everything. If they are rude, answer only the factual part. If they refuse a fair counter or a legal repair outright, say what you will do next, calmly, and then do it (deposit scheme, tenancy board, small claims). Never threaten a step you would not take.
> I'll treat the 14 days as passed on Friday. If the deposit hasn't been returned by then, I'll open a claim with the deposit scheme, which I'd rather avoid. Happy to talk before then.
> I'll leave the tone to one side. The leak was reported on 12 May and is still unrepaired. Please confirm a date this week.

entries.title: Quitting a job, or leaving a group or commitment gracefully
entries.summary: How to leave a job, a board, a group or a volunteer role so people remember the exit as clean and generous.
entries.body:
# Leaving gracefully

## Goal
Everyone you leave behind would work with you again. The exit is short, kind, and leaves nothing hanging.

## Resigning from a job

**Do it in person or by call first, then a short written note.** The written note is a record, not the conversation.

**Structure (conversation):** decision, stated clearly → one line of reason or none → last day → what you'll do to hand over → thanks, specific.

**Script for the conversation:**
> I wanted to tell you directly: I've decided to leave, and I'm giving my notice today. My last day would be the 30th. I've accepted a role that's a step toward [X]. I want to make the handover as clean as possible, so I've started a doc of everything I own and I'd like to spend the next four weeks making sure nothing drops. I've really valued working for you, particularly [specific].

**Written note (email, after the conversation):**
> Hi Maria,
> Following our conversation, this is my formal notice of resignation. My last day will be Friday 30 August. Thank you for the past three years, and especially for backing me on the platform project. I'll make sure the handover is complete before I go.
> Best,
> Dan

**If you're leaving because of problems:** you do not have to say why. "It's time for a change" is complete. Save the honest feedback for the exit interview if you want to give it, and keep it factual.

**If they counter-offer:** "I appreciate that, genuinely. I've made my decision and I'd like to keep it clean. Thank you."

## Leaving a committee, board or volunteer role

> Hi all,
> I'm going to step down from the committee at the end of this term. I've loved being part of it, and I need to free up some time for [X]. I'll finish the [thing I own] before I go and I'm happy to help whoever takes over get up to speed. Thank you for having me.

## Leaving a group chat / social group / regular commitment

> I'm going to step back from Thursday football; my schedule's changed and I keep letting you down on numbers. Thanks for having me, and I'll come to the end-of-season thing.

> Ducking out of this group, my notifications are too much. Message me directly any time, I'm still around.

## Leaving a friend group project or shared commitment (harder)

> I need to be honest with you both: I can't keep up my part of the podcast and I'd rather say it now than fade out. I'll finish the two episodes I owe and hand over the editing files. I'm sorry to let you down on it and I really hope you keep going.

## Principles
- Tell the person most affected first, directly. Not via the group.
- Give a date. Vague exits linger.
- Offer a handover and mean it.
- Do not use the exit to settle scores. You can be honest without being final.
- Do not over-explain the reason. It invites negotiation.
- The last two weeks are what people remember. Work them properly.

## Avoid
- Resigning by text or email only.
- Announcing to the team before telling your manager.
- "I've been unhappy for a long time" as the opener.
- Burning the bridge, even a bridge you never plan to cross.
- Letting things quietly drop instead of formally leaving.

## If they react badly
Anger, guilt or a hard sell to stay all get the same response: hold the decision, keep it short, and do not re-argue the reason. If your manager goes cold for the notice period, keep doing the handover visibly and put it in writing so the record is clean. If a group takes the exit personally, one warm reply, then let it settle. Do not answer hostility with a parting speech.
> I understand this isn't the news you wanted, and I'm not going to change my mind. I do want the next four weeks to be useful, so tell me what you'd like prioritised in the handover.
> I know it leaves a gap for the committee and I'm sorry for that. I'll finish the grant report and brief whoever takes it on. That's what I can do, and I'll do it properly.

entries.title: Cross-cultural and multilingual notes
entries.summary: Adjustments to directness, formality and structure when the other person's cultural or linguistic defaults differ from the user's. General patterns, not stereotypes.
entries.body:
# Cross-cultural and multilingual notes

These are tendencies, not rules. Always weight the individual's own messages over their assumed background. The mirror rule in `02-tone-calibration` still comes first.

## The main dial: directness
Cultures differ most on how explicitly a no, a disagreement or a request is stated.

**Higher-directness defaults** (common in the US, Netherlands, Germany, Israel, Australia): a plain "no" or "I disagree" is normal and respected. Softening too much reads as evasive or unclear.

**Lower-directness defaults** (common in Japan, Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, much of the Middle East, often the UK and Canada in polite registers): a no is often implied ("that might be difficult", "let me think about it"). A blunt no can read as rude; a blunt disagreement can cause loss of face, especially in front of others.

**Practical adjustments**
- Writing to a lower-directness reader: add one sentence of acknowledgement before the point, offer the no as a difficulty or alternative rather than a flat refusal, and never disagree in a group message. Take it private.
- Writing to a higher-directness reader: cut hedges, put the ask in line one, and do not apologise for asking.
- Reading a message from a lower-directness sender: "we will consider it" and "it may be difficult" often mean no. Do not push for a harder answer publicly; ask privately and gently.

## Formality
- Some cultures expect titles and surnames until invited otherwise (Germany, Japan, Korea, much of Latin America in business). When unsure, start formal and mirror their reply.
- Age and seniority carry more weight in many East Asian, South Asian and African contexts. A junior person messaging a senior one should be warmer and more formal than they would be with a peer.
- Emoji, exclamation marks and first names are safe with peers almost everywhere under 40; be more careful with seniors and first contacts.

## Structure
- Some readers expect relationship first, business second (much of Latin America, the Middle East, South Asia): a line asking after them or their family is not filler, it is the message working. Skip it and you sound cold.
- Others expect business first (Germany, Nordics, US business email): the pleasantries can go after the point or be omitted.

## Writing to a non-native speaker
- Short sentences. One idea each.
- Avoid idioms, sarcasm and jokes that depend on wordplay.
- Say the ask plainly; indirect English ("you might want to consider") is often missed.
- Dates in unambiguous form: "14 March", not 3/14.

## When the user is writing in their second language
- Do not "correct" their voice into corporate English. Keep it simple and natural.
- Suggest the version that is easiest to say and to read, not the most sophisticated.
- If they ask for a translation of a diplomatic message, translate the intent, not the words; softeners do not map one to one.

## Avoid
- Stereotyping an individual from their name or location.
- Over-formality as a default; many people find it distancing.
- Assuming English-language norms of directness are neutral. They are not.

entries.title: Money between friends (splitting, owed money, chasing)
triggers: ask a friend to pay me back
entries.summary: How to raise money with friends in a way that treats it as logistics, not character: clear numbers, easy method, no moralising.
entries.body:
# Money between friends

## Goal
The money gets sorted and nobody feels judged. Treat it as admin. The moment it becomes about character, it costs more than the money.

## Structure
1. **Casual opener.**
2. **The number and what it was for**, factual.
3. **The easiest way to pay**, stated.
4. **Optional deadline framed around your needs, not their failing.**
5. **Light close.**

## Principles
- Be specific and fast. The longer a debt sits, the more awkward it gets for both of you.
- Send the number, not a hint. "Whenever you get a chance" is a hint; "£42 for the tickets, here's my link" is a request.
- No shame, no story. They almost certainly forgot.
- If it is a pattern with someone, stop fronting money for them. That is the fix, not a better reminder.
- If you decide to let it go, actually let it go. Do not let it go and then resent it.

## Examples

**First reminder, casual:**
> Hey, whenever you're near your phone: £42 for the gig tickets, my link's [link]. No rush, just so I don't forget.

**Second reminder:**
> Bumping the £42 for the tickets, I've got rent going out Friday so it'd be a help before then.

**Larger amount, direct:**
> Can we sort the £300 from the trip? I've been carrying it a while and it's starting to matter on my end. If it's easier in two chunks that's fine, just let me know when.

**Splitting a bill when someone's underpaying:**
> Let's just split it evenly, it's easier than working out who had what. £28 each.

**Proposing a split before a trip (prevents most problems):**
> Let's do a shared pot for the trip, everyone puts in £200 up front and we settle at the end. Saves the awkward maths.

**Someone asks you to cover them again:**
> I can't front it this time, I'm keeping things tight this month. Can you book your own and we'll meet there?

**Deciding to write it off:**
> Don't worry about the £15, call it even for the lift last week.

## Avoid
- "I hate to bring this up, but..."
- "I'm not made of money, you know."
- Bringing it up in front of others.
- Sarcasm.
- Vague hints ("remember that thing I paid for?").
- Letting it sit for months and then dumping it all at once.
- Sending a payment request app notification with a passive-aggressive memo.

## If they get defensive or keep not paying
If they snap ("it's only £42"), do not explain your finances; agree it is small and repeat the request once. If a third reminder gets nothing, decide: write it off for real, or say plainly that you will not front money again. The pattern is the fix, not a sharper reminder. Never raise it in front of others or through a pointed payment memo, however tempting.
> Yeah, it's not a lot, which is why I'd like to get it done. Link's above whenever you're ready.
> I'll stop chasing the £42. Going forward I'll book and pay separately, no hard feelings, it's just easier for me.

entries.title: Negotiating price, rate or salary
entries.summary: How to ask for more without sounding entitled or apologetic: anchor with a number and a reason, stay warm, and leave room for them to say yes.
entries.body:
# Negotiating price, rate or salary

## Goal
You get closer to your number and the other side still wants to work with you. The tone is collaborative: "how do we make this work" not "give me more".

## Structure
1. **Enthusiasm first, genuine and short.** They need to know you want this.
2. **The gap, factually.** "The offer is at X; based on [market/scope/my last role], I was expecting closer to Y."
3. **Your number, specific.** Not a range (they will take the bottom). Slightly above what you would accept.
4. **One reason**, the strongest, framed as value to them.
5. **Collaborative ask.** "Is there flexibility there?" or "What would it take to get to Y?"
6. **Optional: name what else could move** (start date, equity, title, scope, payment terms) so a no on money is not a dead end.

## Principles
- Never apologise for negotiating. It is expected; not negotiating is the surprise.
- Silence after your number is fine. Do not fill it by lowering your number.
- Anchor with a number; "more" is not a negotiation.
- Reasons about your needs (rent, kids) are weak. Reasons about your value or the market are strong.
- Be the person they want to say yes to. Warm, calm, unhurried.
- Get it in writing before you decline anything else.

## Examples

**Job offer, email:**
> Hi Jordan,
> Thank you for the offer, I'm genuinely excited about the role and the team. I want to be straightforward about one thing: the base is at $95k, and based on the scope we discussed and what I'm seeing for comparable roles, I was expecting closer to $110k. Is there flexibility to get there? If base is fixed, I'd be open to talking about a signing bonus or an earlier review. Either way I'm keen to make this work.
> Best,
> Alex

**Freelance rate, client pushes back:**
> I understand the budget's tight. My rate is $120/hour and that's where I need to be for this kind of work. What I can do is scope it tighter: if we drop [X], I can bring the total under your number. Would that work?

**Client asks for a discount:**
> I don't discount the rate, but I'm happy to find a version that fits your budget. What if we phase it: [smaller scope] now at [price], and the rest when it makes sense?

**Buying something, private seller:**
> I'm interested and can collect this week. Would you take £350? I know it's under asking; that's what I can do in cash today.

**Raise conversation, script:**
> I'd like to talk about my compensation. Over the last year I've [two specific results]. I've looked at the market for this role and I'm below it. I'd like to move to [number]. What would it take to get there?

**They say no:**
> Understood. Can we agree a date to revisit, say six months, with clear goals attached? And in the meantime, is there movement on [other lever]?

## Avoid
- "I was hoping for a little more, if possible?"
- Giving a range.
- Justifying with personal expenses.
- Ultimatums you will not follow through on.
- Accepting on the call. "Let me review the full package and come back to you tomorrow" is always fine.
- Negotiating twice on the same point after they have moved once.

## If they say no or go quiet
A flat no on money is rarely the end. Move to the other levers you named, and get a date. If they go silent after your counter, wait two working days, then send one short nudge that keeps the offer warm.
> Thanks for looking into it. If the base can't move, could we agree a review at six months with the target in writing, plus the earlier start date? That gets me to a yes.
> Just checking in on the compensation question so I can give you a firm answer by Friday. Happy to talk it through on a call if that's easier.
If they withdraw the offer over a polite counter, that tells you something useful.

entries.title: Out of office and away messages
triggers: back from holiday reply to customer
entries.summary: Auto-replies for vacation, parental, sick and sabbatical leave, a shop closed for a holiday, a freelancer at capacity, plus the message to send a customer once you are back.
entries.body:
# Out of office and away messages

## Goal
The sender knows in ten seconds whether to wait, go elsewhere, or escalate, and they do not feel brushed off. You get to be away without a pile of "did you see this?" follow-ups.

## Structure
1. **Dates.** When you left, when you are back, in the sender's terms ("back Monday 12 October").
2. **What happens to their message.** Read on return, not read, or forwarded.
3. **Who to contact instead**, with one route each: urgent versus everything else. Name a person, not "the team".
4. **One line of warmth or context** if it fits you. Optional.
5. **Nothing else.** No apology, no list of what you are doing on holiday.

## Principles
- Under 60 words for most. Auto-replies get skimmed on phones.
- Be honest about whether you will read it. "I'll reply when I'm back" is a promise; only make it if you will.
- Give the cover person a heads-up before you name them, and put their name in exactly one place.
- Humour works when it is one line, self-directed, and does not delay the information. It fails when it is the whole message, mocks the sender, or forces them to hunt for the dates.
- For sick leave and bereavement, give less detail, not more. "Away for a few weeks" is enough. Your colleagues can say more if they need to.
- Small businesses: put the reopening date and how to order in the meantime. Customers mostly want to know if they can still buy.
- Freelancers at capacity: an "away" reply is still a sales message. Give the next available date and make it easy to book it.

## Examples

**Vacation, standard:**
> I'm away until Monday 12 October and not reading email. For anything urgent, Nadia Weiss (nadia@[company]) is covering. Everything else, I'll reply in the week I'm back.

**Vacation, with humour that does not backfire:**
> I'm out until 12 October, somewhere with patchy signal and excellent bread. Nadia (nadia@[company]) has my projects until then; I'll reply to everything else when I'm back.

**Parental leave:**
> I'm on parental leave until early February and won't be checking this inbox. For [product] questions, please contact Jordan Reyes (jordan@[company]). For everything else, hello@[company] will route you. Thanks for your patience.

**Sick leave (keep it minimal):**
> I'm on leave for a few weeks and not reading email. Please contact Amir Haddad (amir@[company]) for anything active. Messages here won't be forwarded, so do resend if it's important.

**Sabbatical:**
> I'm on sabbatical until March 2027 and this inbox is closed. Client matters: Priya Nair (priya@[company]). Speaking or press: office@[company]. If it can wait until spring, I'd love to hear from you then.

**Small business closed for a holiday (email):**
> We're closed for the holidays from 23 December, reopening Monday 5 January. Online orders still go through and ship from the 5th. Anything ordered before the 20th has already shipped. Thanks for a great year.

**WhatsApp or Instagram away status for a shop:**
> Closed for the holidays, back Tue 6 Jan. Order online any time at [link]; we'll reply to messages when we reopen.

**Freelancer at capacity:**
> Thanks for getting in touch. I'm fully booked until mid-November, so I can't take new work before then. If your timeline allows, reply with a line about the project and I'll hold a slot for the week of 17 November. If you need someone sooner, I'm happy to suggest a name.

## Avoid
- "I have limited access to email." Either you read it or you do not.
- Listing everyone in the department with a topic each.
- "Sorry for any inconvenience." Being away is not a fault.
- Jokes about how much you hate work, or about the sender's timing.
- Leaving the auto-reply on after you return.
- Detailed medical or family information in a sick-leave reply.
- Forgetting the date format: "back on the 5th" means nothing on the 27th of another month.

## When you are back
Send this to a customer who wrote during the closure, before they have to chase:
> Hi Elena, thanks for your message on the 28th, and thanks for waiting while we were closed. I've checked and the order is in stock; it'll ship today and you'll have tracking by this evening. If anything else came up in the meantime, I'm here.
If you cannot fix it immediately:
> Thanks for your patience over the break. I'm back today and I'm looking at this first thing; you'll have a proper answer from me by tomorrow noon.
If someone is annoyed they had to wait:
> That's fair, a week is a long time to wait for a reply. I'm on it now and I'll have it sorted by [time]. Thanks for sticking with us.

entries.title: Announcing a price increase, delay, closure or policy change to customers
triggers: tell customers prices are going up
tell clients my rate is increasing
entries.summary: Customer-facing announcements that keep trust: the news early and plain, the reason in one line, what stays the same, what customers can do, and a real person's name.
entries.body:
# Announcing a price increase, delay or change to customers

## Goal
Customers feel informed and respected, not blindsided or spun. Most people accept a change; they do not accept feeling tricked.

## Structure
1. **The change, in the first sentence.** Date and amount.
2. **The reason, one honest line.** Costs, wages, quality. Not a paragraph.
3. **What isn't changing** (quality, service, the thing they love).
4. **What they can do**: lock in the old price, cancel easily, get help.
5. **Thanks, and a real name.**

## Principles
- Early. Give real notice (30 days is standard; more for big changes).
- Plain. "Prices are going up 8% from 1 March" beats "we're adjusting our pricing structure".
- No apology for a fair increase. "Sorry" makes people think you're doing something wrong.
- Make the exit easy. Customers who can leave easily are more likely to stay.
- Send it from a person, not "The Team".
- Do not over-justify. Every extra reason invites debate.

## Price increase

**Small business, email to customers:**
> Hi Sam,
> From 1 March, our prices are going up by about 8%: the medium candle moves from $28 to $30, and the large from $42 to $45. This is the first increase in three years and it covers what wax and shipping now cost us. Nothing about how we make them changes. If you'd like to stock up at current prices, the old prices hold on the site until the end of February. Thank you for keeping a small business going.
> Ana

**Freelancer, to an existing client:**
> Hi Rob,
> I'm updating my rates for the new year. From 1 January, my day rate moves from $600 to $680. For you, I'll hold the current rate through March so it doesn't affect the project in flight. I'm grateful for the work we've done together and I'm looking forward to more of it.
> Nina

**Subscription service:**
> Your plan is changing from $9 to $11 a month from your next billing date after 1 April. Since you've been with us a while, you'll stay at $9 until July. You can cancel any time from your account page, no hoops. Here's what the extra covers: [two lines].

## Delay

> Hi Sam, your order #4521 is going to arrive later than promised: the new estimate is 22 May, about a week late. A supplier issue on our side, not yours. If that doesn't work for you, reply and I'll refund it in full, no questions. Otherwise, I'll send tracking the moment it ships. Sorry for the wait.
> Ana

**Bigger delay, many customers:**
> We've hit a manufacturing delay and orders placed since 1 May will ship around 10 June instead of the end of May. If you'd rather not wait, reply to this email for an immediate full refund. If you can wait, we'll add [small make-good] to your order. We'll email again the day it ships. Thank you for your patience, and I'm sorry.

## Closure or ending a service

> After six years, we're closing the shop on 30 September. It's a personal decision, and a good one for us, but we'll miss this. Between now and then: everything's 20% off, gift cards can be used until the 30th (email us if you can't make it), and we'll help you find a new supplier for anything you regularly order. Thank you for six extraordinary years.

## Policy change (returns, hours, minimums)

> From 1 June, our return window changes from 60 days to 30. Anything ordered before 1 June keeps the 60-day window. The reason: returns after a month were mostly worn items we can't resell, and it was costing more than we could absorb. Everything else about returns stays the same: free label, fast refund.

## Avoid
- "Due to unforeseen circumstances."
- "We regret to inform you."
- Hiding the number.
- Sending it from "no-reply".
- Blaming customers or "some people".
- Burying the change in a newsletter.

## If customers push back
A few will reply annoyed or threaten to leave. Answer each one personally, restate the change once, do not re-argue the reason, and make leaving genuinely easy. Most people who are given a graceful exit stay.
> Hi Sam, I understand, and I'd rather you told me than quietly went elsewhere. The new price is what it costs us to keep making these properly, so it stands. If it no longer works for you, I'll cancel today with no fuss, and you'd be welcome back any time.
If someone is rude, stay factual and short. One reply, then let it rest. Do not offer a secret discount to the loudest person; the others will hear about it.

entries.body:
# Apologising publicly as a brand or small business

## Goal
Affected customers feel told the truth and taken care of, and everyone else sees a business that owns its mistakes. A public apology is mostly information. "Sorry" appears once, early; the rest is what you did, what you are doing and what changes.

## Structure
1. **What happened, plainly, first sentence.** "Our site was down for six hours on Tuesday."
2. **Who was affected and how.** Numbers if you have them.
3. **Sorry, once, from a named person.**
4. **What you have already done.**
5. **What affected customers get and how**, automatic where possible.
6. **What changes so it does not repeat.** One or two specifics, not a "full review".
7. **How to reach a human.**

## Principles
- Speed over polish. A short honest post within hours beats a lawyered statement in three days.
- Match the size. A wrong price needs three sentences. A data incident needs a full email and a pinned post.
- Promise only what you can verify. "Never again" is unkeepable. "A second check before prices go live" is not.
- Do not name or blame an employee publicly. Own it as the business.
- For a data incident, check your legal obligations on notification timing and content in every region where you have customers before you post, and say plainly what data was and was not involved.

## Examples

**Outage, social post:**
> Our checkout was down from 9am to 3pm today and about 1,200 of you couldn't place orders. Sorry, that's on us: a failed update, now rolled back. Anything ordered today ships free, code TODAY until Sunday. Charged without a confirmation? Email me at [address] and I'll sort it within the day. Jo, founder.

**Bad batch, email to buyers:**
> Subject: Your order from batch 0417 and what we're doing
> Hi [first name],
> The hot sauce you ordered between 2 and 9 April came from a batch that didn't ferment properly. It's safe, but it tastes flat and some bottles separate. I'm sorry. A replacement ships this week at no cost, no action needed. If you'd rather have a refund, reply "refund" and it's done. We now test every batch before bottling rather than every third one.
> Kemi

**Rude employee, reply to a public complaint:**
> I've read your post and I'm sorry that's how you were spoken to on Saturday. That's not the standard here and I've dealt with it. I'm sending you a DM now to refund your visit and invite you back as my guest. Thank you for telling us rather than just not coming back. Ana, owner.

**Pricing mistake, post:**
> For about 18 hours yesterday our site showed the leather tote at $19 instead of $190. We've honoured all 340 orders placed at that price; they ship next week. Sorry to anyone who saw it change mid-checkout. A second sign-off now sits before any price goes live.

**Data incident, email (check your legal obligations first):**
> Subject: A security incident affecting your account
> Hi [first name],
> On 12 June we found that an unauthorised person accessed a database containing customer names, email addresses and order history between 3 and 11 June. It did not contain passwords or payment details, which are stored separately and were not accessed. I'm sorry. We closed the access within two hours, reset all internal credentials and brought in an outside security firm. Be cautious of emails claiming to be from us that ask for payment or login details; we never ask for those by email. Questions: reply here or call [number]. We'll update you by [date].
> Marco, CEO

**Social media misstep, pinned post:**
> Yesterday's post was thoughtless and it hurt people. It's down. Sorry, no excuses: it shouldn't have been written or approved. From now on two people sign off on every post. Comments are open and we're reading.

**Pinned comment under the apology:**
> Affected and not heard from us by Thursday? Email [address] with your order number and I'll reply personally. Jo.

## Replying to angry comments under the apology
Silence under your own apology looks like you posted and ran. Reply to each specific comment briefly and move detail to DM: "You're right, and I'm sorry. Sending you a DM now to fix your order." If a comment is wrong on the facts, correct once, calmly: "The outage was six hours, not two days. Anyone who ordered that day gets free shipping, including you." If a commenter is abusive, one reply, then stop. Do not delete unless it breaks the platform's rules or yours.

## Avoid
- "We apologise for any inconvenience."
- "Mistakes were made."
- "We take this very seriously."
- "Some customers may have experienced."
- Blaming a vendor, a platform or a junior employee in public.
- Promising a "full internal review" with no specifics.
- Posting and going silent.
- Deleting critical comments.

## If it goes badly
If the apology gets more heat than the original problem, do not apologise for the apology. Reply to comments with actions taken and let the fixes speak. If someone says "words are cheap", agree: "Fair. Here's what's done so far: [two actions]. I'll post an update on [date]." Then post it on that date.

entries.title: Pushing back on your boss
entries.summary: How to say no or "not like this" to a manager while sounding like someone who is protecting the outcome, not avoiding the work.
entries.body:
# Pushing back on your boss

## Goal
Your manager sees you as someone who raises problems early with options attached. Not someone who says no, and not someone who silently drowns.

## Structure
1. **Align with the goal.** "I want to get this done well."
2. **The constraint, factual.** "Right now I have A, B and C due this week."
3. **The trade-off, made visible.** "If I take this on, one of them slips."
4. **Options, two or three, with your recommendation.**
5. **Ask them to choose.** This is the key move: you are not refusing, you are asking them to prioritise.

## Principles
- Never a bare no. Always "here's what it would take" or "here's what has to give."
- Bring the trade-off to them; do not make it yourself and hope they do not notice.
- Raise it as early as possible. Pushback on day one is planning; pushback on the deadline is failure.
- Be specific about time. "This is a two-day job" beats "this is a lot."
- Written follow-up after a verbal conversation, so the decision is on record.

## Examples

**Unrealistic deadline, chat or email:**
> I can get this done, but not to the standard we'd want by Thursday. To do it properly is about three days. Options: I deliver a rough version Thursday and the polished one Monday; or I push the Marsh report to next week and give this my full time. My recommendation is the first. Which do you prefer?

**Too much on your plate:**
> Quick priority check. I've got the launch deck, the Q3 numbers and the onboarding doc all due this week and I can realistically do two well. Which one can move? My suggestion is the onboarding doc, since it's internal.

**Disagreeing with a decision:**
> Can I flag a concern before we commit? I think [decision] risks [specific problem] because [reason]. If we've already weighed that, I'll get on board. If not, [alternative] might get us the same result with less exposure.

**Being asked to do something outside your role, repeatedly:**
> I've been picking up the invoicing for a few months now and I'm happy to help in a pinch, but it's now about four hours a week that's coming out of [core work]. Can we either make it official and rebalance, or move it back to finance?

**Pushback on a weekend request:**
> I can't do this weekend, I've got commitments I can't move. I can start first thing Monday and have it to you by noon. If it truly can't wait, let's talk about what else comes off my plate.

**Written follow-up after agreeing:**
> Just confirming what we agreed: I'll deliver the rough version Thursday and the final on Monday, and the Marsh report moves to the 14th. Shout if I've got any of that wrong.

## Avoid
- "That's not my job."
- "I'm too busy."
- Saying yes and then missing.
- Complaining about workload without a proposed fix.
- Pushing back in front of their boss or the team.
- Making the decision for them silently.

## If they insist anyway
Sometimes the answer is "all of it, by Thursday". Do not argue a second time. Say what will slip, confirm it in writing, and deliver what you said you could. The written record is what protects you when the deadline hits.
> Understood, I'll make Thursday the priority. To be clear, that means the Marsh report moves to next week and this version will be rough rather than polished. I'll send it by 4pm.
If the pattern repeats every week, raise it separately in a one-to-one as a capacity problem, not a single-task problem: "Can we look at my load overall? I'm at about 130% and I'd rather we fix that than keep triaging."

entries.title: Reconnecting after a long silence
entries.summary: How to message someone you have not spoken to in months or years without the awkwardness swallowing the message.
entries.body:
# Reconnecting after silence

## Goal
Make the gap a non-issue in one sentence, then give them something specific and easy to respond to.

## Structure
1. **Name the gap lightly**, once. Do not apologise for it at length; they went quiet too.
2. **A specific reason you thought of them** (a memory, something you saw, a real update).
3. **One easy question** about them, or one low-stakes invitation.
4. **No pressure to reply fast.**

## Principles
- Most people are relieved, not annoyed, when an old friend reaches out. The awkwardness is mostly yours.
- Do not open with a favour. If you need something, reconnect first, ask in a later message or say the ask plainly and separately.
- Do not try to catch up on everything in the first message.

## Examples

**Old friend, text:**
> It's been about two years, which is absurd. I walked past that ramen place we used to go to and thought of you. How are things? No rush, just wanted to say hi.

**Former colleague, LinkedIn or email:**
> Hi Ana, long time. I saw the news about your move to [company] and wanted to say congrats, it looks like a great fit. If you're ever up for a coffee, I'd love to hear how it's going.

**Someone you drifted from after a falling out (no big conversation, just warmth):**
> Hey. I've been thinking about you lately and hoping you're doing well. No agenda. If you ever want to grab a coffee, I'd like that.

**Reconnecting because you need something (be honest):**
> I'll be upfront that I'm reaching out because I could use your advice on [X], and I feel a bit sheepish since we haven't talked in ages. Either way, I've thought about you and hope you're well. If you have 20 minutes some time, I'd be grateful; if not, no hard feelings at all.

## Avoid
- "Sorry I've been such a bad friend" (makes them console you).
- A wall of updates about your life.
- "We should catch up sometime!" with nothing concrete.
- Reconnecting only when you need something, without acknowledging it.

## If they reply warmly
Suggest one specific thing within two messages: a call this week, a coffee on a named day. Momentum dies otherwise.

entries.body:
# Replying to a customer inquiry in DMs

## Goal
Answer the question in the first line, then move them one step closer to buying or booking, without pressure. DMs are conversations, not tickets.

## Structure
1. **Answer first.** Price, availability, yes/no. Do not make them ask twice.
2. **One useful extra** they did not ask but will want (sizes, delivery time, what's included).
3. **The next step**, specific and easy: a link, a question that moves toward a decision, an offer to hold it.
4. **Their name if you have it, no sign-off.**

## Principles
- Speed is the biggest lever in DMs. A fast "yes, $45, here's the link" beats a perfect reply an hour later.
- Match their energy. If they wrote two words, don't write two paragraphs.
- Never "DM for price" style evasions. Give the number.
- Ask one question, not three. Each question is a hurdle.
- If they go quiet after a price, one gentle follow-up in 24 to 48 hours, then stop.
- Sound like a person. No "Thank you for reaching out to us!"

## Examples

**"How much is this?"**
> Hi Jess! That one's $45, and it comes in the green and the oat colour. Free shipping over $60. Want me to send the link, or hold one for you?

**"Is this still available?"**
> Yes, still here! It's the last one in medium. I can hold it till tomorrow evening if you want; just say the word.

**"Do you do custom orders?"**
> We do! Custom pieces start at $120 and take about two weeks. Tell me roughly what you're thinking and I'll give you a proper quote.

**"Can you tell me more about the workshop?"**
> Of course. It's Saturday the 14th, 2 to 5pm, at the studio in Peckham. $80 includes all materials and you leave with a finished piece. Beginner-friendly, max eight people. There are three spots left; want me to save you one?

**Service business, "are you free next week?"**
> I've got Tuesday 10am or Thursday 2pm free next week. Either work? If not, send me a couple of times and I'll make one fit.

**Follow-up after silence (once):**
> Hey Jess, just checking whether you'd like me to keep holding the green one; totally fine if you've gone off it.

**They ask for a discount:**
> I don't discount individual pieces, but if you grab two the shipping's free, and there's a 10% code for newsletter sign-ups. Want it?

**Question you can't answer immediately:**
> Good question, let me check with the maker and come back to you by tonight.

## Avoid
- "Thanks for reaching out! Please visit our website for more information."
- Copy-paste templates that ignore their actual question.
- Three questions in one reply.
- Emoji overload.
- Hard-sell pressure ("only 2 left, buy now!!").
- Leaving inquiries unanswered for a day.

## If they go quiet or get rude
Silence after a price is normal; it is not a no. One follow-up (see above), then leave it. If they come back in a week, greet them as if no time has passed. If someone gets rude about the price or the wait, keep it short and polite, and do not defend the number.
> That's the price for these; no hard feelings if it's not for you. Thanks for asking.
If they argue further or start insulting you, stop replying. You do not owe a debate in your inbox, and a calm last message is what any onlooker will see.

entries.title: Requesting an introduction or referral
entries.summary: How to ask someone to use their relationship for you: make it zero-effort with a forwardable blurb, give them an out, and report back.
entries.body:
# Requesting an introduction or referral

## Goal
Your contact can forward one message and be done. The ask costs them almost nothing and puts their reputation at minimal risk.

## Structure
1. **The ask, in the first line.** Who, and why them.
2. **Why it's a reasonable intro** (what you offer the other person, not just what you want).
3. **A forwardable blurb**, separate paragraph, written in third person or as a self-introduction they can paste.
4. **A real out.** They may not be close enough, or may not want to spend the capital.
5. **Promise to report back.**

## Principles
- Double opt-in: the best intros ask the other person first. Make it easy for your contact to do that by giving them the blurb.
- Never ask for an intro to someone you could just email yourself. Use intros for people who would otherwise ignore you.
- Be specific about the ask you'll make of the other person. "A 20-minute call about X" not "pick their brain".
- Report back. People stop making intros for those who vanish afterward.
- For referrals (jobs), make it explicit they can say no without explanation; their name is on the line.

## Examples

**Intro request, email or DM:**
> Hi Jo,
> Could I ask a favour? I'd love an intro to Dana Park at Helix. I'm building a tool for exactly the onboarding problem she wrote about last month and I think a 20-minute conversation would be useful for both of us. If you're not close enough for that to be comfortable, no worries at all, just say.
>
> If you're up for it, here's a blurb you can forward:
>
> "Dana, I'd like to introduce Sam Lee. Sam runs Northstar, which builds guest-checkout tools for e-commerce, and has some interesting data on the onboarding drop-off you posted about. Sam's asked for 20 minutes to compare notes; happy to connect you if you're open to it."
>
> I'll let you know how it goes either way. Thanks, Jo.
> Sam

**Job referral, to a friend at the company:**
> Hey, I'm applying for the senior designer role at your place. Would you be comfortable referring me? Totally understand if you'd rather not put your name on it; we've never worked together directly, so I won't take it personally. If yes, I'll send you the job link and a two-line summary to make it painless.

**Asking a former manager for a reference:**
> Hi Priya, I'm in the final round for a role at [company] and they've asked for references. Would you be willing to be one? They'd call for about 15 minutes, sometime next week. If you're not able to, no problem, I'd just appreciate a quick heads-up so I can ask someone else.

**Reporting back (do not skip this):**
> Quick update: Dana and I spoke on Tuesday, really useful, and she's introduced me to their platform lead. Thank you for making that happen; I owe you a coffee.

## Avoid
- "Do you know anyone who could help me with...?" (vague, makes them do the thinking).
- Asking for multiple intros at once.
- Not providing a blurb.
- Following up on the intro with your contact more than once.
- Asking for an intro and then not using it.
- Forgetting to close the loop.

## If they say no or don't reply
A no on an intro is about their relationship with the other person, not about you. Thank them and keep the door open. If they do not reply at all, one nudge after a week, then find another route; two chasers makes them avoid you.
> No problem at all, thanks for letting me know. If it ever feels like a better fit down the line, I'd still be glad of it.
> Hi Jo, resurfacing this in case it got buried. Totally fine to say no, I just want to know whether to try another path.
If they make the intro and it goes nowhere, still report back. Silence after their effort is what stops the next intro.
